An error message of "failed to load" is not always a missing file. It can have several different causes:
1) the file is indeed missing
2) the file has a wrong Capitalization: A.png and a.png are two different files for a browser, only Windows has an override that loads the wrong file if it exists.
3) the filename contains a symbol that is not allowed under networking rules - only latin letters, arabic numbers and very few special signs are allowed. SPACE on the other hand is forbidden, which is why it is usually replaced by underscore _ on internet files.
4) the foldername of any folder in the entire filepath contains a forbidden symbol. Example:
c:\folder\test folder\project\img\actor.png
can cause a failed to load "img\actor.png"
That is the reason why for example space is replaced by %20 in a browser adress line if you open local files - the browser simply can't handle space, not even in internal error messages. And that %20 override doesn't always work.
So basically if the cause for the error is something else or if there are two causes for the error, then replacing the file will not stop the error message.

not if the folderpath itself contains a forbidden letter.
Windows tries to force the browsers to access files through overrides in such cases, and those overrides do not always work.
Theoretically it is even possible that the local play can fail - in early versions of MV this was often the case, until the programmers made the playtest automatically use a virtual folder that would be guaranteed not to use the physical folderpath on the HDD.
Only after that change the playtest hadn't those failed to load errors for wrong foldernames anymore.
But a deployed playtest has to use the physical folderpath and can come against that problem.

posts.body:
I am not entirely sure if this is the problem causing your first issue, but in your posted code you have:
JavaScript:
if (this._isError = true)
This is most likely not what you meant to do as you are setting this._isError to true rather than comparing this._isError to true. You need to use 2 or 3 equal signs to compare things.
For your second issue, it is a simple logic error. Currently, you have:
JavaScript:
var ConsoleMsg = parameters["Show in Console?"] == "false";
Let's consider what would result from this code when the parameter is set to "false" or "true".
When the parameter is set to "false" you have told it to compare that against "false", so your variable will be set to true, because "false" is equal to "false". However, when the parameter is set to "true" it will compare that against "false" and the result will be false, because "true" is not equal to "false".
